About us

Synup is where marketing agencies and multi-location brands run their local marketing. Manage listings, reputation, social media, local SEO, and AEO for every client or location from one hub. Agencies get full white-labeling, so the experience stays under your brand. Sydekick, Synup's AI agent, handles the repetitive work across all of it. Teach it your playbooks and it manages the day-to-day the way your team would, so you can grow your client base or location count without growing headcount to match. Most teams replace five or more tools when they switch. Every plan includes every feature, and pricing scales with the locations you manage, not the features you unlock.

      Putting your logo on the report is the easy part of white-label reputation management. What decides whether the service works is everything behind the logo: who handles the reviews every day, when the client steps in, and what happens when a review needs an escalation. If nobody agrees that at sign-up, the first angry review sits unanswered while everyone assumes someone else has it. Niladri Sarkar, our CMO, walks agencies through it: → Start with one package your team can deliver every month → Agree a responsibility matrix: your agency owns delivery, the client owns the facts, the vendor provides the software, the publisher decides what shows → Get two named contacts per client for escalations → Write the client's brand rules down, and keep a person approving every reply → Run the same trial checklist on every vendor, Synup included The guide, the responsibility matrix and the trial checklist are in the comments. #WhiteLabel #ReputationManagement #MarketingAgency

      A one-star review lands at one of your locations. Marketing sees it. The branch manager sees it. Customer service hears about it. Who replies? If nobody has agreed, you get one of two outcomes: two replies to the same review, or none at all. Niladri Sarkar, our CMO, walks through how multi-location brands decide who owns the reply: → First decide: answer now, get facts from the branch, or escalate → Escalate reviews that mention a lawyer, an injury, a safety issue, discrimination, a named staff member, or health or account details → Give one person ownership of the reply, with a named approver and a backup → Promise only what's been confirmed → Check the reply actually published The full guide and an ownership and escalation worksheet are in the comments. #ReviewManagement #ReputationManagement #MultiLocationMarketing

      The listing is live and customers can find the location. What the team can't say is who controls the Google Business Profile now that the owner or agency has left. Before any request, keep three things apart: the Google Account you're signed in with, the role it holds on the profile, and the exact location the record covers. If you can't see the access list, write “unknown.” Then choose the route: – Primary owner reachable: invite the successor, let them accept, check the seven-day restrictions on primary-ownership changes and other selected actions for newly added owners and managers, then have the primary owner transfer and check the result from the successor's own sign-in. – Owner unreachable: use the request route for your business type and log every response. An accepted invite is not an ownership transfer, and Google's three-day owner window is not a recovery date. Guide and an inventory CSV with hypothetical example rows: https://lnkd.in/eQPMNCUN Video: https://lnkd.in/eewxg8Qe

      Picture a local search where the map shows three businesses and the AI answer above it names six, including all three. Did the map predict the answer? Every map business made the answer: 3 of 3. Half the answer came from outside the map: 3 of 6. Both statements are true, because they start from different lists. This is a hypothetical to show the arithmetic, not a measured page. When you report overlap, write down which list you started from and how many items it had.

      Niladri Sarkar breaks down key findings from Synup's massive AI In Local Search study covering 53K+ Google Results across 49 business categories and 250 US cities. In our September 2026 desktop data, the map pack appeared on 91–97% of pages across four query families. AI Overviews ranged from 4% of “near me” pages to 75% of “best” queries naming a specific service or attribute (that last group comes from a 50-city subset). Watch the video for the findings and a practical way to check what customers see: • Compare “near me,” category + city, “best,” and “best” plus a specific service or attribute. • Look beyond map rank to the whole page: AI Overviews, business cards, cited sources, ads and discussion results. • Benchmark reviews against the businesses that actually appear for each phrasing. Full study, charts and methodology in the first comment.
